questions.question: In Ladder Logic, what is the functional difference between an Examine if Closed (XIC / Normally Open -| |-) contact and an Examine if Open (XIO / Normally Closed -|/|-) contact?
options: XIC evaluates True when its associated memory bit is 1 (energized); XIO evaluates True when its associated memory bit is 0 (de-energized).
XIC can only control AC motors, while XIO controls DC relays.
XIO causes an instant hardware fuse burnout when triggered.
XIC is forbidden in industrial safety standards.
questions.correctAnswer: XIC evaluates True when its associated memory bit is 1 (energized); XIO evaluates True when its associated memory bit is 0 (de-energized).
questions.explanation: XIC checks for presence of signal (1/True); XIO checks for absence of signal (0/True).
questions.learningObjective: Master fundamental Ladder Logic Boolean contacts.

questions.question: In PLC Hardware, I/O Addressing & Scan Cycles, why is an electrical 'seal-in' (latching) branch contact wired in parallel with a momentary Start push-button?
options: To keep the motor starter coil energized through the motor's own auxiliary contact after the momentary Start button is released.
To double the operating voltage supplied to the PLC power supply.
To invert the rotation direction of a 3-phase induction motor.
To prevent the Emergency Stop button from functioning.
questions.correctAnswer: To keep the motor starter coil energized through the motor's own auxiliary contact after the momentary Start button is released.
questions.explanation: Seal-in logic latches the output coil high until an unlatch condition (like Stop or overload trip) breaks the rung continuity.

questions.question: In PLC Hardware, I/O Addressing & Scan Cycles, a field proximity sensor is connected to a PLC input module. The sensor's onboard LED lights up when metal is present, but the PLC input status LED remains OFF. What is the most probable electrical cause?
options: A sinking/sourcing mismatch (e.g., an NPN open-collector sensor connected to a Sinking PLC input module that requires a PNP current source).
The PLC ladder logic code has a syntax indentation error.
The PLC baud rate is configured to 9600 baud instead of 115200.
The factory floor lighting is reflecting off the machine frame.
questions.correctAnswer: A sinking/sourcing mismatch (e.g., an NPN open-collector sensor connected to a Sinking PLC input module that requires a PNP current source).
questions.explanation: Sinking modules require a sourcing (PNP) field device to provide +24V, whereas sourcing modules require a sinking (NPN) device to complete the circuit to 0V common.
questions.learningObjective: Troubleshoot sinking and sourcing (NPN vs PNP) industrial I/O circuits.

questions.question: What is the operational behavior of an On-Delay Timer (TON) instruction when its rung input condition changes from False to True?
options: The timer accumulates time (ACC increments). When ACC reaches Preset (PRE), the Done (.DN) bit turns True and remains True until rung input goes False.
The Done (.DN) bit turns True immediately, and turns False after the preset duration expires.
The timer executes an emergency CPU halt.
The timer counts down backward from 32767.
questions.correctAnswer: The timer accumulates time (ACC increments). When ACC reaches Preset (PRE), the Done (.DN) bit turns True and remains True until rung input goes False.
questions.explanation: A TON instruction delays the energization of its output; the Done bit asserts only after the rung condition has remained True for the full preset duration.
questions.learningObjective: Analyze On-Delay Timer (TON) timing diagrams and bit states.

questions.question: A 4–20 mA pressure transmitter measuring 0 to 10 bar is connected to a 12-bit unipolar analog input module (0 to 4095 counts). What raw digital count corresponds to a process pressure of 5 bar (12 mA)?
options: 2048 counts (or approximately 50% scale)
4095 counts
512 counts
1024 counts
questions.correctAnswer: 2048 counts (or approximately 50% scale)
questions.explanation: 5 bar is 50% of the 0–10 bar range. At 50% span (12 mA), the raw 12-bit digital count is 50% of 4095 = 2047.5 ~ 2048 counts.

questions.question: In a manufacturing cell, two rungs in the same PLC program write to the exact same physical output address (e.g., O:1/0). The first rung evaluates True, but the second rung evaluates False. What will be the actual physical state of the output terminal?
options: The physical output will be OFF (de-energized), because the PLC writes output states based on the last evaluated rung during the scan cycle.
The physical output will oscillate continuously at 100 kHz.
The physical output will be ON (energized), because True always overrides False in hardware.
The PLC CPU will trigger a fatal divide-by-zero exception.
questions.correctAnswer: The physical output will be OFF (de-energized), because the PLC writes output states based on the last evaluated rung during the scan cycle.
questions.explanation: This is a classic 'Duplicate Coil' defect. The PLC logic executes sequentially from top to bottom; the last rung to evaluate controls the final output image table written to field hardware.
questions.learningObjective: Identify and eliminate duplicate coil race conditions in PLC programs.

questions.question: How does an Output Latch (OTL) coil differ from an Output Energize (OTE) coil in Allen-Bradley / IEC ladder logic?
options: OTL remains retentively ON even if rung logic goes FALSE, until an explicit Output Unlatch (OTU) instruction executes.

It permanently locks the PLC in STOP mode.

questions.question: In ladder logic, what happens when a Master Control Reset (MCR) zone is de-energized (FALSE)?
options: All non-retentive outputs (OTE) within the MCR boundary are forced OFF, regardless of individual rung conditions.
The CPU enters fatal hardware fault mode.
All timers inside the zone freeze their accumulated values permanently.
Inputs are inverted.
questions.explanation: When an MCR zone is false, the controller skips execution of rungs within the zone and forces all non-retentive output coils OFF as a safety and interlock mechanism.

questions.question: What is the operational behavior of Jump (JMP) and Label (LBL) instructions in PLC ladder diagrams?
options: When the JMP rung is TRUE, the PLC skips scanning all intermediate rungs and resumes execution immediately at the target LBL.
JMP restarts the program from the beginning of memory.
JMP causes an asynchronous interrupt.
LBL outputs an analog 4-20 mA current.
questions.explanation: JMP allows conditional branching: when true, execution jumps to the designated LBL, skipping rungs in between to optimize scan time or bypass inactive machine modes.

questions.question: How are modular subroutines invoked in ladder programs using JSR instructions?

Subroutines run on separate hardware microprocessors.
Subroutines can only be called from HMI touchscreens.
JSR is executed only once when the PLC powers up.
questions.explanation: JSR calls a modular ladder routine, passing execution to the subroutine until a return (RET) instruction transfers execution back to the main ladder scan.

RTO does not have a Done bit.

RTO cannot exceed 10 seconds duration.

questions.question: How are two timers cascaded in ladder logic to create an automatic continuous flasher or periodic pulsing circuit?

By connecting timer coils in parallel across 230V AC.
By setting timer presets to negative values.
Cascading timers is impossible without external microcontrollers.

Square root instruction only.

Frequency, amplitude, and wavelength.

By converting temperature to radio waves.

questions.question: How does an industrial Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) receive real-time target motor speed references from a PLC analog output module?
options: Via a 0-10V DC or 4-20 mA signal wired to the VFD analog input terminals, where 0-10V corresponds linearly to 0-50/60 Hz.
Through discrete relay contacts only.
By varying main AC supply frequency at the circuit breaker.
Through pneumatics.
questions.explanation: The PLC DAC card outputs 0-10V or 4-20 mA into the VFD's speed potentiometer terminals, varying motor stator frequency and rotational speed.
